newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's beleaguered PM faces tough winter.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's beleaguered PM faces tough winter.

text.p: Bulgarian Prime Minister Zhan Videnov faces a tough battle to keep his Socialist Party (BSP) united through a harsh winter of economic misery after the opposition's resounding win in Sunday's presidential race.
As Bulgarians brace for big price rises and possible bread and fuel shortages, the ruling party of ex-communists has vowed to review some of its policies and to listen more to voters.

Petar Stoyanov, a reformist lawyer, trounced the Socialists' Ivan Marazov, winning 60 percent of the vote in Bulgaria's second post-communist presidential poll. Incumbent Zhelyu Zhelev, also a liberal, did not seek reelection.

Although the president is a largely ceremonial figure he has veto powers that Zhelev has frequently wielded while in office to halt what he regards as Socialist efforts to curb media freedom and private land ownership.
"In the coming weeks we will see BSP attempts to retain their grip on power by such devices as cabinet reshuffles," said Evgenii Dainov of the Centre for Social Practices.

Other analysts said the party might try to invite members of other smaller parties into a coalition government to broaden their support. The BSP has an absolute majority in parliament and the next parliamentary elections are not due until 1998.
Videnov, 37, said he would call an emergency meeting next week to discuss the party's next moves and a BSP congress will take place in January. He has not ruled out cabinet changes.
BSP sources and Western diplomats played down talk of an impending party breakup into reformist and hardline camps.
"We need debate, not party splits," a constitutional lawyer from the BSP's reformist wing, Georgi Bliznashki, told Reuters.
"The important thing is to change our style of leadership. We must become more responsive to the public," he said.

Videnov, a former communist youth leader, is often accused by the Bulgarian media of being too aloof and authoritarian. His party's links to powerful, shadowy economic groupings have also drawn sharp criticism.
"It is not so much that hardliners are holding up reforms. The problem is corruption, the power of vested interests in or close to the BSP," said one Western diplomat.
Noting that the BSP had inherited the old communist regime's instincts for unity, the diplomat added: "The odds still seem to be against a major split."

Ironically the depth of Bulgaria's economic crisis could help keep Videnov in office as further political turmoil would risk driving the lev currency through the floor and delay plans to close or sell off state firms.
Ministers are locked in crucial talks this week with a visiting mission of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), trying to unblock loans to meet looming foreign debt repayments.

Bulgaria's political instability -- it has seen six revolving-door governments since the bloodless overthrow of communist dictator Todor Zhivkov in November 1989 -- has badly hampered its tortuous transition to a market economy.
Valentin Vatsev, a political analyst close to Videnov, noted that Bulgaria's political situation on Monday was essentially the same as it was before the election.
"The government retains its control of parliament and the opposition keeps the presidency," he told state television.
Vatsev said he hoped Stoyanov would cooperate with the government over its reforms. Zhelev and Videnov, old political rivals, are not even on speaking terms.

Stoyanov, who has accused the Socialists of embarking on market reforms only under heavy IMF pressure, sent a conciliatory message to Videnov on Sunday and mooted a National Salvation Council to help combat the economic crisis.
